title: Novice mistress
hook: how do you tell someone a truth they don't want? Thérèse guiding the young nuns, and a neighbor's answer
tomorrow: a nun who never leaves writes to men across the world. why?

segments.voice: Yesterday, throwing flowers: small sacrifices nobody sees, tossed like petals out of love. Your line was petals. Today Thérèse gets a job where small things won't stay hidden.

Performance reviews. Group project post-mortems. The friend who says be honest, do I look okay, and means please don't be. Most of us lean one way: blunt and right, or kind and vague. Near the end of her life, Thérèse was handed a job she never asked for: help form the novices, the young women just entering Carmel, one of them her own sister. You can't avoid a novice. You eat with her, pray with her, sweep beside her. So how do you tell someone a truth she doesn't want to hear?
screen: `BE HONEST. (PLEASE DON'T.)` → `A JOB SHE NEVER ASKED FOR.` → `A TRUTH SHE DOESN'T WANT.`

segments.voice: Her answer starts with her limits. In Manuscript C she says she saw at once the job was beyond her strength. So she threw herself into God's arms like a little child, and told him she was too small to feed his children; he would have to fill her little hand. Then the honest part. She couldn't care whether the novices liked her, she writes. If she needed their affection, she'd stop telling them the truth about their faults, and be no help at all. So she told them, even when it cost her. Then the kind part. No two souls could be led the same way, so she met each one where she was. Saint Paul's phrase in the Douay-Rheims fits her method: "doing the truth in charity." A neighbor tradition says something close. In the Pali Canon, talking with a prince named Abhaya, the Buddha says he speaks words that are true and helpful, even when unwelcome, and that he knows the right time to say them. The prince has a baby on his lap, so the Buddha asks: if the child put a pebble in its mouth, wouldn't you take it out, even if it drew a little blood? Yes, says the prince, out of compassion. What they share: the truth told for the other's good, with care for the timing. The honest difference: the Buddha speaks from his own awakening. Thérèse says she had nothing of her own to give. Jesus had to fill her hand.
screen: `TOO SMALL: FILL MY HAND.` · `NO NEED TO BE LIKED.` · `EACH SOUL LED DIFFERENTLY.` · `THE PEBBLE IN THE BABY'S MOUTH.` · then, large: `HONEST AND KIND.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one kind truth someone near you needs to hear. Say it once, softly, out loud, and listen to it: is it true, does it help them, is now the time? Then rest with it while the sit runs, and let the words get gentler if they need to.
Novice mistress. The role Thérèse filled in practice near the end: guiding young nuns with the truth, told kindly.
Here's the line: honest and kind, one thing and not two, the way Thérèse led. See you soon.

howItsDone: In religious orders an experienced sister forms the novices in prayer and community life, and Catholics often read Thérèse's Manuscript C for how she guided them with honest, gentle correction.

fork.setup: your best friend asks you to read her college essay. it's full of clichés and due in three days. what would Thérèse with her novices do?
options: tell her now, specifically and gently, while there's time to fix it.
say it's great; she's stressed and needs encouragement more than notes.
quietly rewrite it for her, so she never has to hear it's weak.
fork.reveal: Thérèse said that if she needed to be liked, she'd stop telling the truth and be no help. the truth, fitted to the person and the timing, is the kind thing.

chat.meaning: Thérèse wouldn't trade the truth for being liked, and she fit it to each novice. Honest and kind aren't opposites when the truth is for the other's good.

notes: Index title 'Novice mistress': Thérèse did not formally hold the title (Mother Marie de Gonzague kept it; Thérèse assisted). The trapdoor says so; the word segment says 'the role Thérèse filled in practice'. Keeper to confirm.

Paraphrased from Manuscript C; confirm: she saw the task was beyond her strength, threw herself into God's arms like a little child, said she was too little to feed his children and asked him to fill her little hand; she could not seek to be loved or she would fail to tell the truth; souls must each be led differently. Her sister among the novices is Céline (unnamed in the script); confirm.
Ephesians 4:15 Douay-Rheims (Challoner) wording to confirm; offered as fitting her method, not as her citation.

Unity thread (wisdom day): MN 58, Abhayarajakumara Sutta, paraphrased (no public-domain translation the validator lists): the Tathagata speaks what is true and beneficial, even if unwelcome, knowing the proper time; the simile of the baby with a stick or pebble in its mouth, removed even if it draws blood, out of compassion. Some translations say 'a stick or a pebble'; confirm. Honest difference stated: the Buddha speaks from his own awakening; Thérèse says Jesus had to fill her hand. Ask a Buddhist reader whether the paraphrase and the difference are fair; no ranking intended.
